analysis.one_liner: Raises the top income tax rate to 39.6% and deposits the extra revenue into Social Security and Medicare trust funds.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee until the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have undone a piece of the 2001 tax cut for the very highest earners, raising the top income tax rate back to 39.6% starting in 2002. Every dollar of the added revenue would have been deposited into the Social Security and Medicare (Hospital Insurance) trust funds. It was introduced by Rep. Barney Frank and 16 other Democrats but was never considered by the committee that handles tax bills.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, current and future Social Security and Medicare beneficiaries would have gained a modestly stronger funding base, since the new revenue was earmarked directly to the trust funds that pay their benefits. Taxpayers with middle and lower incomes would have paid nothing, because the increase applied only to the highest tax brackets.

how_it_helps.text: The bill raised the top individual income tax rate to 39.6%, applying it across the top three rate tiers (38.6%, 37.6%, and 35.0%) created by the 2001 tax cut, effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2001.

All of the added revenue was appropriated to the Social Security trust funds — the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance fund, the Disability Insurance fund, and the Hospital Insurance (Medicare) fund — transferred at least quarterly from the general fund.
Because the change applied only to the highest rate brackets, taxpayers below the top brackets would have seen no rate increase.

analysis.who_pays: The highest-income individual taxpayers — households in the top tax brackets — would have paid roughly 1 to 4.6 percentage points more on their top-tier income. That includes wealthy wage earners and some owners of pass-through businesses (like partnerships and S corporations) who pay personal income tax on business profits.

drawbacks.text: Some owners of pass-through businesses — partnerships and S corporations that pay tax on the owner's personal return — would have faced the higher top rate on business income, not just on salaries, which critics of top-rate increases generally cite as a burden on small business.

Depositing general revenue into the trust funds improves their ledgers but does not fix the underlying math of Social Security and Medicare, which depends on payroll taxes versus benefit costs; earmarked income-tax revenue is a supplement, not a structural repair.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a straightforward trade: a modestly higher tax on the very highest incomes in exchange for dedicated funding for Social Security and Medicare. The cost would fall entirely on top-bracket taxpayers; the benefit — additional trust fund revenue — is real but incremental, since the amounts involved (a fraction of one rate tier's revenue) would not by themselves close Social Security or Medicare's long-term funding gaps. It was a statement bill about tax fairness rather than a comprehensive fix.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and stayed there; the committee never held a hearing or a vote, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Barney Frank introduced the bill on September 21, 2001, joined by 16 original House Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day — the committee with jurisdiction over income tax rates — and received no further action.
Thirty House Democrats eventually cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Top-bracket taxpayers came out ahead: the lower top rates set by the 2001 tax cut stayed in place for the rest of the Congress, and no trust-fund deposit from this source was made. The Republican majority on Ways and Means also avoided having to vote on a tax increase.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Top-bracket taxpayers; the bill died unheard

for.name: Rep. Barney Frank
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise the top rate to 39.6% and route the revenue to the Social Security and Medicare trust funds.

for.name: 30 of 208 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors in the House of Representatives
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including 16 original cosponsors named at introduction.

against.name: Rep. Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the tax-writing committee, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it without committee action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 30 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill went no further than the Republican-chaired Ways and Means Committee.

industries.note: The bill would have raised the top rate by 1 to 4.6 percentage points on their top-tier income, solely to fund the Social Security and Medicare trust funds. Its defeat preserved the lower top rates enacted in the 2001 tax cut.
Business income reported on owners' personal returns would have been taxed at the higher top rate. The bill's defeat kept their top marginal rate at the post-2001-cut level.
